Yet that is exactly what has happened in Elsebeth Schröder's research group at the Division of Quantum Device Physics.

more.summary: The European Union has committed to achieving climate neutrality by 2050, a process that will require rapid and substantial reductions in greenhouse gas emissions across all economic sectors.

more.title: Laser experiments recreate solar flare physics and reveal consistent magnetic reconnection rates
more.summary: Magnetic reconnection is a process that occurs when the magnetic fields of a conductive plasma quickly rearrange and release massive amounts of stored magnetic energy. It is widely thought to be the underlying mechanism behind cosmic events such as solar flares and substorms in Earth's magnetosphere.

more.title: Giving students a voice in how they learn could transform the classroom experience
more.summary: Research from Queen Mary University of London explores how combining learner autonomy with student-led inquiry can create a more engaging and collaborative experience for international students learning academic English.

more.title: Mathematicians Build Long-Awaited Graph Sandwich
more.author: Paulina Rowińska
more.summary: The proof of a decades-old conjecture has given researchers a new way to understand complex networks. The post Mathematicians Build Long-Awaited Graph Sandwich first appeared on Quanta Magazine

more.title: Improving urban flood forecasting with real-time hazardous rainfall detection
more.summary: The Korea Institute of Civil Engineering and Building Technology (KICT) announced that it will apply its early detection technology for quasi-stationary linear rainbands and sudden localized torrential rainfall to the Urban Flood Forecasting Platform operated by the Han River Flood Control Office in Korea for urban flood forecasting.

more.title: Who benefits from tariffs, according to research
more.summary: Tariffs are usually debated as trade policy. But a study from the University of Chicago Booth School of Business treats them as something else: a mechanism for redistributing wealth.

more.title: Discovery of CRISPR's long lost ancestor may expand gene-editing toolkit
more.summary: CRISPR may be a powerful technology for gene editing, but the system existed in bacteria long before scientists began using it. For billions of years, CRISPR has acted as a natural immune system in bacteria and other microbes, helping defend them against invading viruses.

more.title: Background hums and buzzes affect human behavior, researcher finds
more.summary: Have you ever stopped and listened to the background sounds in a room you are in? The hum of the ventilation? The buzz of electricity? While most of the time we are barely aware of these sounds, Arthur Jinyue Guo, a researcher at the RITMO Centre for Interdisciplinary Research on Rhythm, Time and Motion, has revealed that they nevertheless affect our behavior.

more.title: Anti-transgender legislation can cause psychological distress even in states with trans-friendly laws
more.summary: Legislation that affects or discriminates against transgender and gender-diverse individuals can cause more psychological distress than personal experiences of discrimination, according to new Virginia Commonwealth University research published in the journal American Psychologist.

more.title: The art heist paradox: Why better police work can lead to more stolen masterpieces
more.summary: When a multimillion-dollar masterpiece vanishes from a museum, the public calls for tougher criminal penalties and better-funded police task forces. But research from Wake Forest University suggests that some of these intuitive solutions can backfire, resulting in more art crime, not less.

more.title: From the start, the solar system chose fire over ice to build its first bodies
more.summary: When the solar system first took up the task of building solid bodies—such as planets, moons and protoplanets—it basically had a choice between two ingredients: heat-forged chondrules, which were millimeter-sized bits of rock, and matrix, a fine-grained, cold dust loaded with water ice and organic molecules. And from the get-go, the solar system chose fire.

more.title: How rural policing gaps can make escaping domestic violence harder
more.summary: Before murdering Molly Ticehurst in April 2024, court documents show Daniel Billings had threatened to exploit the limits of policing in her country town: "I will come in the middle of the night … The police won't stop me. I will get to you quicker than they will."

more.title: Inertia co-founder Jeff Lawson’s next big bet is fusion: Go inside it at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026
more.author: TechCrunch Events
more.summary: Inertia co-founder and CEO Jeff Lawson joins the Smart Systems Stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026. Register now to save up to $200 by September 25.

more.title: Peer sexual harassment emerges early, highlighting need for prevention before Grade 4
more.summary: Sexual harassment between peers begins as early as Grade 4 and continues throughout lower secondary school. Most of those who sexually harass others have also experienced harassment themselves. These are among the findings of a doctoral thesis in psychology by Aziz-Kaan Dönmez from the University of Gothenburg, who studied peer sexual harassment among Swedish children and adolescents in Grades 4–9.

more.title: Scientists discover cells that cheat death and rebuild damaged tissue
more.summary: Scientists discovered a population of cells that can start the process of programmed cell death, survive it, and then help rapidly rebuild damaged tissue. Their descendants become far more resistant to future damage, revealing a mechanism that could improve healing but may also help cancers return after treatment.

more.title: Scientists just named a new snake after Guns N’ Roses legend Slash
more.summary: A newly discovered snake from New Guinea has been named after Guns N’ Roses guitarist Slash, who has loved reptiles since childhood. Genetic testing and physical differences confirmed that the reddish-brown groundsnake, Lielaphis slashi, is a species scientists had never formally recognized before. The nonvenomous snake may use large rear teeth to catch slippery lizards and reptile eggs.

more.title: NASA’s Moon orbiter finds a 728-foot crater that wasn’t there before
more.summary: NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter has revealed a 728-foot-wide crater that formed on the Moon in 2024, making it the largest newly formed crater ever identified in the solar system. The impact disturbed the surface for miles around it, creating a surprisingly large cold zone and showing how dramatically a single collision can reshape the lunar landscape.

more.title: A startup that builds other startups raised $100M and is all-in on physical AI
more.author: Kirsten Korosec
more.summary: UP.Labs, now doing business under the name Vantora, is building startups for industrial corporations.

more.title: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope could last more than twice as long as planned
more.summary: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope may now have enough fuel for at least 22 years of science, more than double its original 10 year design life. An extremely precise course correction, extra fuel at launch, and additional expected savings could keep the powerful observatory studying the universe for decades.

more.title: Medieval Chinese skeleton may reveal first evidence of a brutal punishment
more.summary: Ancient Chinese authorities used many creative ways to punish people, often with methods designed to mark them for life. One brutal example mentioned repeatedly in historical texts is cutting off a person's nose. However, archaeologists in China have never found skeletal evidence to prove that it occurred.
